html:
Bevy is the most active Rust game engine. Its defining idea is ECS (Entity Component System): data lives in components, behaviour lives in systems, and the engine schedules systems to run in parallel wherever they do not conflict.

Version note: Bevy's API changes quickly (roughly quarterly). The examples below target the 0.15/0.16 era (Camera2d and Sprite as components, required components instead of *Bundle). If something does not compile, check the migration guide for your version — that is normal in Bevy, not a mistake on your part.

Setup

The first build compiles ~400 crates and takes several minutes. After that, incremental builds are seconds.

The smallest game

Read that as: "on startup, create a camera and an entity with a sprite and a Spinner marker; every frame, rotate everything with a Spinner."

Query<&mut Transform, With<Spinner>> is a system parameter — Bevy uses the type to decide which entities match and, because the types declare access, it can run non-conflicting systems in parallel on different threads.

ECS in one page

Concept Meaning
Entity an ID. Nothing else. Cheap to create and destroy
Component a plain struct of data attached to an entity
System a function that reads/writes components
Resource a singleton, like Time or your Score
Query a typed filter over entities and their components
Schedule an ordered set of systems (Startup, Update, FixedUpdate)

Movement and input

Spawning and despawning

commands are deferred: they apply at a synchronisation point, not immediately. That is why you can despawn an entity you are still iterating over.

Combat: a system that touches two queries

UI: text and score

Res<T>::is_changed() is the cheap way to skip work when nothing happened — Bevy tracks change detection per component and per resource.

Fixed timestep for physics

Use FixedUpdate for physics and game logic that must be deterministic; use Update for input, animation and UI. Mixing them causes the classic "jumps higher on a fast machine" bug.

Assets and hot reload

Assets are loaded by path and return a Handle. In debug builds Bevy watches the assets directory and hot-reloads on save — a large quality-of-life win.

Performance notes

Symptom Cause Fix
Low FPS with few entities per-frame allocation reuse buffers, avoid format! in Update
Frame spikes asset loading on the main thread preload in Startup, use AssetServer states
Systems not parallel one system queries &mut everything split into narrower queries
Huge binary default features default-features = false, enable only what you need

Ecosystem

Crate Purpose
bevy_rapier2d / bevy_rapier3d physics
avian2d / avian3d ECS-native physics (newer alternative)
bevy_egui immediate-mode debug UI
bevy-inspector-egui live entity inspector — invaluable
bevy_asset_loader declarative asset loading states
leafwing-input-manager action-mapped input
bevy_kira_audio audio
iyes_progress loading screens

Install bevy-inspector-egui on day one. Being able to see and edit every component live saves hours.

Honest assessment

Good: data-oriented architecture, hot reload, excellent 2D, no GC pauses, strong community momentum, compiles to WASM and native.

Costs: API churn between versions, compile times, a smaller asset store than Unity, and 3D is less mature than 2D.

When to pick it: a 2D game, a prototype where you want determinism and no engine licence, or a game whose logic you want to unit test.

When not to: a large 3D title on a deadline, or a team of artists who need Unity/Unreal tooling.

Exercises

  1. Build the spinning-sprite example and add WASD movement.
  2. Add a Score resource, an Hit event, and a system that increments the score when an enemy's health reaches zero.
  3. Move physics into FixedUpdate at 60 Hz and verify behaviour is frame-rate-independent by capping the frame rate to 30.
  4. Add a bevy_egui debug window showing entity count.
  5. Split one fat &mut Transform system into two narrower systems and check with the inspector that they run in parallel.
  6. Disable default features and enable only 2D + UI; measure the binary size difference.
